In [[statistics]], the '''Hannan–Quinn information criterion (HQC)''' is a criterion for [[model selection]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hannan |first1=E. J. |last2=Quinn |first2=B. G. |date=1979-01-01 |title=The Determination of the Order of an Autoregression |url=https://academic.oup.com/jrsssb/article/41/2/190/7027596 |journal= Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology|volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=190–195 |doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1979.tb01072.x |issn=0035-9246|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It is an alternative to [[Akaike information criterion]] (AIC) and [[Bayesian information criterion]] (BIC). It is given as

: <math> \mathrm{HQC} = -2 L_{max} + 2 k \ln(\ln(n))\ </math>

Where:

* ''<math>L_{max}</math>'' is the log-likelihood, 
* ''k'' is the number of [[parameters]], and 
* ''n'' is the number of [[observations]].

According to Burnham and Anderson, HQIC, "while often cited, seems to have seen little use in practice" (p. 287).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Burnham |first1=Kenneth P.  |title=Model selection and multimodel inference: a practical information-theoretic approach |last2=Anderson |first2=David Raymond |last3=Burnham |first3=Kenneth P. |date=2002 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-95364-9 |edition=2nd |location=New York |oclc=ocm48557578}}</ref>  They also note that HQIC, like BIC, but unlike AIC, is not an estimator of [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]].  

[[Gerda Claeskens|Claeskens]] and [[Nils Lid Hjort|Hjort]] note that HQC, like BIC, but unlike AIC, is not asymptotically [[Efficiency (statistics)|efficient]]; however, it misses the optimal estimation rate by a very small <math>\ln(\ln(n))</math> factor (ch. 4).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Claeskens |first1=Gerda |title=Model selection and model averaging |last2=Hjort |first2=Nils Lid |date=2008 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-511-79048-5 |series=Cambridge series in statistical and probabilistic mathematics |location=Cambridge}}</ref> They further point out that whatever method is being used for fine-tuning the criterion will be more important in practice than the term <math>\ln(\ln(n))</math>, since this latter number is small even for very large <math>n</math>; however, the <math>\ln(\ln(n))</math> term ensures that, unlike AIC, HQC is strongly consistent. It follows from the [[law of the iterated logarithm]] that any strongly consistent method must miss efficiency by at least a <math>\ln(\ln(n))</math> factor, so in this sense HQC is asymptotically very well-behaved.  

Van der Pas and Grünwald prove that model selection based on a modified Bayesian estimator, the so-called switch distribution, in many cases behaves asymptotically like HQC, while retaining the advantages of Bayesian methods such as the use of priors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van der Pas |first1=Stephanie |last2=Gruenwald |first2=Peter |date=2018 |title=Almost the Best of Three Worlds: Risk, Consistency and Optional Stopping for the Switch Criterion in Nested Model Selection |url=http://www3.stat.sinica.edu.tw/statistica/J28N1/j28n111/j28n111.html |journal=Statistica Sinica |doi=10.5705/ss.202016.0011|arxiv=1408.5724 }}</ref>
